name: Jade Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI companies, unions and government. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary workday involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and have a bachelor’s degree and a professional accountancy qualification. I have spent years preparing repair-shop accounts and tax returns at this firm; I know the ordinary cases, while our senior handles the hard disputes. I like matching an invoice to a delivery note, and I dislike being asked to sign a figure I cannot trace.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life like after you shut the file?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Malik, my partner, fixes buildings, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is about normal for this accountant role, we have roughly three months of expenses saved, and some similar firms are nearby. I have never used AI tools; I prefer a process a colleague can demonstrate on a closed file before it touches a client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the software can add a small check if it shows me which repair invoice it used. I would still sign only a return I can explain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our mortgage is manageable on two steady wages and we have about three months of expenses saved. A small office shortcut does not put my job at risk, but I do not like checks whose source I cannot see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep reconciling repair-shop accounts with the signed paper checklist my supervisor uses. In the first year I would ask for a paid old-file demonstration if the firm makes a new check compulsory in writing, but I would not open an AI tool on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the mortgage and wary of a needless new office routine. I can learn a required check when someone shows the source.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did the checklist help recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tyre shop had two invoices with the same number, and the list made me check the delivery dates before filing. A neat screen would not have settled which tyre order belonged in that year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask in the demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask which original invoice the software used and where the reviewer signs. I have never used AI tools, so I would need the senior accountant beside me on a closed file.

I would sign only a **return I can explain**.
think: Our **three-month cushion** and steady wages keep us secure in a mild change.
I mistrust checks without a **visible source**.
do: Keep reconciling **repair-shop accounts** with signed checklist and source invoices.
Take a **paid old-file demonstration** only after a written compulsory job rule.
feel: I feel **calm** about income while cautious about new office routines.
S0.quote: A neat screen would not have settled which tyre order belonged in that year.
fieldNote: Her **tyre invoice story** explains why she wants a source trail rather than a polished screen.
She has **never used AI** but would learn a compulsory approved check through paid supervised practice on a closed file.

steps.text: Keep reconciling repair-shop accounts using signed source-invoice checklist
Take paid old-file AI demonstration only after written job rule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the manager to name who checks the software draft when a tyre shop questions a tax return. I would also ask for the hours plan before a colleague disappears from the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is account checks and tax notes, so my paid hours could shrink as software takes them. Three months saved and some other firms nearby give me a choice, but the mortgage still needs both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for the staffing plan in writing and keep reviewing the assigned accounts. If the approved checker becomes a written requirement, I would take paid training on closed files with a senior beside me; in the first year, if my hours are cut, I would apply for a posted accounts role at the repair depot only with a written salary, hours and start date that preserve our mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible pay cut, not certain that it will happen. I would rather keep my current job than move on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the depot role workable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The start date must let me keep my present pay until the new wage begins, and the shift must fit pickup for our younger child. My partner Malik does building maintenance and cannot promise an early finish every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test the checker at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the client records belong at work and I do not know the tool. I would practise only during paid office hours with the senior reviewing each result.

do: Keep **assigned accounts** and request a written staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2028 reaches the accounts and tax desks in 2028, before capable robots arrive around 2031. The manager should tell us whose files remain and when shifts end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my account checks to go because cheaper AGI can do the thinking, and my job may end. Three months of savings would help briefly, but Malik’s hands-on maintenance could face robots later, so I cannot assume two wages stay safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for written cut dates and cancel our planned paid city break before the deposit is due, keeping that money for bills. If my accounting post ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply to posted salaried depot-finance jobs only with written salary and a start date that keeps the mortgage current; if no suitable vacancy is open, I would keep any paid files at the firm and ask Malik about confirmed extra maintenance shifts with school pickup arranged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing a wage before we can settle into another job. Three months of savings is not a long bridge when two jobs may change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can Malik get extra shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Malik can cover urgent building repairs sometimes, but the manager must confirm the hours and paid rate. We would ask my sister to collect our younger child on those evenings before counting the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would need a named paid vacancy and written start date. A trial cannot cover a mortgage payment, however polite the offer sounds.

S2.quote: Three months of savings is not a long bridge when two jobs may change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the firm AGI by 2031 gives us time to see whether clients still pay for a person to check awkward invoices. The robots around 2034 do not move our desk deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let me build more cash and get better at checking disputed bills, but I expect routine account work to shrink in 2031. I would need a real paid role rather than a hopeful new title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask my manager for a paid hour each month to review disputed tyre-shop invoices with the senior accountant, if the client agrees. I would deposit 85 a month into savings while both wages hold; in the first year after 2031, if my routine hours fall, I would take a vacant paid dispute-checking post only with written salary, hours and a start date that preserves our mortgage pay, or keep current paid files while seeking posted local work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the wage, but five years lets me test the work without quitting. A written vacancy would count more than a training badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the invoice dispute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the delivery note with the two invoice dates, then let the senior check my conclusion before we call the shop. I know the ordinary books but still need help with tricky cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the client will not pay for the review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the account reviews I have and stop calling it a new service. I would not give the firm unpaid evenings to make a bad idea look viable.

I would remind staff **2034 robots** come after the desk change.
think: Routine **account work** may shrink in 2031 despite my experience.

feel: I feel **anxious** about future pay, with time to test a paid task.
S3.quote: A written vacancy would count more than a training badge.
fieldNote: Her **monthly test** uses a real delivery note under senior review and stops if the client will not pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to pay down the mortgage and find out which clients still pay for checked explanations. Capable robots around 2039 may change Malik’s building work later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could leave us with a smaller loan and older children if both wages hold. Routine desk checks still face AGI in 2036, so I would not treat my current title as protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep reviewing repair-shop returns and ask the manager for paid quarterly disputed-invoice checks with senior review if clients agree to a fee. I would hold six months of expenses in cash before paying an extra 100 monthly against mortgage principal while both wages hold; in the first year after 2036, if routine hours fall, I would stay only if paid client checks cover my salary, or accept a posted local job only after a written wage, start date and school-compatible shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the decade’s end, but our next few years of work and mortgage payments look steady. I would count paid repair-shop renewals before treating invoice checks as a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you the checks pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count how many repair shops pay again next quarter and whether the fees cover my hours. If they do not, I would stop the extra service and keep ordinary paid files while there are any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Malik to take more work now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, he already covers enough building calls and takes our younger child to sports twice a week. I would not add a shift unless the pay is confirmed and we have another ride.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because routine accounts work could go while we still owe on the house. Written cut dates, a real paid vacancy and a school-compatible start would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who shows the tyre shop why its two matching invoice numbers mean different things. A neat total is not the same as an answer.

headlineQuote: A neat total is not the same as an answer.
portrait: At **43**, Jade is an experienced accountant with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification who handles repair-shop accounts.
She and **partner Malik** have two school-age children, a mortgage, typical pay and roughly three months saved.
She has **never used AI** and wants signed sources and paid old-file demonstrations; some local firms are available.
The **2028 scenario** threatens routine checks; longer runways allow supervised dispute work and conditional debt reduction.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her routine account-checking work before another paid post is ready.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written cut dates**, a real paid vacancy and a school-compatible start.
